notes: Each character has only their own lines. User-selected casting: Clay as Cassian, Kendall as Ada. Previous Brodie/Joanna samples were tests and are not approved for inclusion in the full episode. Wade narration and Hallie Ninja voice unchanged.

events.text: By the time Ninja reached Bellwether, the rain had settled into the kind of steady drizzle that didn't feel dramatic enough to deserve a weather warning.
It simply got into everything.

The hills around the village disappeared and reappeared behind the mist. Old stone walls followed the narrow road between fields. An elderly sheep watched her car pass with an expression of deep personal disappointment.
Yeah, you and me both.

She had been driving for hours, with two bags in the back, one paperback on the passenger seat, and a cardboard box she hadn't managed to put away. The box held a chipped blue mug, a packet of photographs, and a key that no longer opened anything she owned.
At the village entrance, a weathered wooden sign announced BELLWETHER — WELCOME.
She almost laughed.
It was such an innocent word. Welcome. As though arriving somewhere was the difficult part.
She found the building above the bakery on her second attempt. The owner, a woman called Ada, opened the door before Ninja had managed to ring the bell.
You must be the new guest.
That depends. Does the room have a bed?
Usually.
Then yes. Definitely me.

Ada gave her an assessing look, but it wasn't the look Ninja had grown accustomed to. No careful lowering of the eyes. No flicker of recognition at a surname. No searching her face for evidence of whether today was a good day to mention her brother.
Just a woman in a cardigan holding a door.
Upstairs, then. You'll find the kettle by the window. Mind the third step. It makes a noise like a dying goose.
I've lived with worse.
Oh, haven't we all.

Ninja carried her bags up. The room was small, clean, and slightly crooked. A quilt covered the bed. The window looked over a wet street with a florist, a repair shop, and the dark-red door of a pub at the far corner.
She placed her things down.
She didn't unpack. Not her clothes, not the box, not even the phone charger.
Unpacking made a place feel like a decision. Right now, the best she could manage was an address.
She pulled on her black jacket, checked the room key twice, and went back out.
Unfamiliar silence had a habit of bringing familiar voices with it.
And hers already sounded like Cassian's.

If I unpack, it means I'm staying. If I stay, somebody will eventually ask why I came. And what am I supposed to tell them? That I drove halfway across the country because every street back home still knows his name?
The first time Cassian taught her to throw a punch, Ninja was eight years old.
It happened behind the building where they lived, on a patch of cracked concrete that somebody optimistically called a courtyard.
She had come home with blood on her knee, dirt on her sleeve, and the fierce conviction that she had won an argument with a boy twice her size.
Cassian, thirteen and already wearing the tired expression of somebody responsible for too many things, sat her on the bottom step.
Tell me what happened.
He was being an idiot.
That's a condition, not an explanation.
He took my bag.
And you?
I took it back.
Cassian glanced at the split skin on her knuckles.
With your face?
Shut up.
He laughed, despite trying not to. Then he cleaned her knee with water from a bottle, tearing a strip from an old cloth when they ran out of proper bandages.
She hissed when the cold water touched the scrape.
Hold still, menace.
You're pulling my leg off.
Yes. That's the treatment. All doctors do it.
When he was done, he crouched in front of her and held out his hands.
Okay. Here's the important part. If somebody bigger than you starts trouble, you don't have to stand there and prove you're fearless.
I wasn't scared.
Then you should've been. Fear can be useful.
She hated that answer.
Cassian tilted his head.
Look at me. Nin. Being brave isn't the same as being stupid.
You're stupid.
Frequently. That's how I've gathered all this wisdom.
He showed her how to stand with her feet steady and how to move away from someone trying to grab her. He made her practise until she stopped trying to win and started paying attention.
Good.
Can I punch you now?
Absolutely not.
She punched his arm anyway.
He looked gravely offended.
That evening they ate toast for dinner because the cupboards were nearly empty. Cassian put the better-looking pieces on her plate and insisted he preferred the burnt ones.
Years later, she would remember that lie more clearly than almost anything he ever taught her.
On her tenth birthday he came home with a supermarket cake in a cardboard box and a candle shaped like the number seven.
That's not my age.
That's because you're a very advanced seven-year-old.
I'm ten.
Then you're an extremely immature ten-year-old. Blow it out.
He'd earned the money washing windows and had forgotten the candle until the shop was closing. She knew that much because his hands smelled of cleaning fluid. She also knew he hadn't eaten lunch.
She divided the cake into two uneven pieces and pushed the larger one toward him.
Birthday law. You get the big piece.
My birthday. My rules.
He looked at the piece, then at her.
You're becoming dangerously difficult.
Good teacher.
He bowed his head in mock defeat.

There was no party. Nobody remembered to put music on. But Cassian sang so badly that the neighbor banged on the wall, and she laughed until she nearly fell off her chair. For years afterward, when a birthday felt disappointing, he'd remind her they still had the record for the most complaints during a single birthday song.
Their home wasn't always dangerous. Sometimes somebody cooked and the radio played old songs. Other nights, voices came through the walls and doors slammed hard enough to rattle the glasses.
Ninja learned to listen for footsteps. Cassian learned to turn up the television and invent a game whenever the footsteps became too loud.
On one particular night, when she was eleven and he was sixteen, the house finally went quiet long after midnight.
She found him sitting on the floor outside her bedroom.
Why are you out here?
Guard duty.
From what?
Spiders. Very serious threat.
There aren't any spiders.
Exactly. You're welcome.
She sat beside him. They said nothing for a while.
Eventually she leaned against his shoulder, and he rested his cheek on her head.
One day, we're going to have a place with doors that only slam when we want them to.
Why would we want them to slam?
Because you'll be annoyed with me.
I'm already annoyed with you.
See? We've got a promising future.
She slept easier that night.
Not because the world had become safe, but because someone had stayed outside the door.
Cassian wasn't an angel.

He forgot appointments. He borrowed things and returned them in odd places. He could turn a five-minute errand into a two-hour adventure, usually involving somebody's broken car and an extremely unconvincing explanation.
When Ninja was fifteen, he forgot the afternoon they'd planned to see a film together. She waited at the cinema entrance for forty minutes before walking home alone.
He arrived later, wet from rain, carrying two paper bags of takeaway and a look that was halfway between guilt and fear of what she'd do to him.
I know.
Wonderful. Saves me explaining.
The van at work broke down.
Did the van also break your phone?
No. That was me being an idiot.
Finally, a diagnosis.
He put the bags on the table.
I was wrong. I'm sorry.
Ninja held on to her anger for another few seconds, mostly out of principle.
Then she opened the bag.
Did you get extra chips?
Do I look suicidal?
She tried not to smile.
He saw it anyway.
As they grew older, Ninja started taking care of him, too: saving him dinner, warning him when people took advantage, and occasionally dragging him out of trouble.
One evening he came home exhausted and collapsed on the sofa. She put on a dreadful action film they'd seen a dozen times.
Halfway through, he opened one eye.
Didn't we agree this movie was terrible?
Yes.
Why are we watching it?
Because you know how it ends.
He was quiet for a moment.
Then he reached down and squeezed her shoulder.
That was how they understood each other. Not through grand speeches or permanent agreement. Through the mundane evidence of being there.
A second mug made without asking.
A text when someone got home.
The comfortable insult that meant, I'm happy you're alive.
Ninja believed there would always be someone who could turn the worst day into something survivable.
She'd built her idea of home around that belief.
Sometimes, when Ninja worked the late shift, Cassian met her at the bus stop. She always claimed she hadn't asked him to. He always replied that he was waiting for the bus himself.
At midnight? You don't even take this route.
Maybe I've developed an interest in public transport.

She'd walk beside him under the streetlights, telling him about difficult customers and coworkers who treated the coffee machine like a complicated medical procedure. He'd listen, ask just enough questions to prove it, and occasionally threaten to buy a more competent coffee machine himself.
Once, when she had a terrible week and couldn't decide whether to laugh or scream, he brought her a packet of biscuits and sat beside her on the curb until she could breathe normally.
He didn't demand a story. He was good at that.
She never realized that eventually he would need someone to sit beside him in the same way—and that he'd become too frightened to ask.
The changes in Cassian began small enough to make excuses for.
A shift that ran long. An unfamiliar car outside the apartment. His phone lighting up at dinner and his smile disappearing before he answered.
He was in his twenties by then, and Ninja had her own life, her own work, her own habits. They didn't account for every hour of each other's days.
Still, she knew the difference between ordinary tiredness and the kind of tiredness that made somebody listen to the hallway before opening the door.
One evening he came over with groceries and left a thick envelope on her kitchen counter.
What's that?
Rent. And a bit extra.
She looked at him.
I pay my own rent.
I know.
Then why are you paying it?
Because you spent half your childhood eating the worst toast ever made, and I'd like to correct the historical record.
She didn't touch the envelope.
Cass.
Nin.
Where did it come from?
Work.
What work?
The boring kind.
You'd complain about boring work. You complain when your socks are too boring.
He smiled, but it didn't reach his eyes.
Seriously. It's fine.
She pushed the envelope back.
I don't need you to buy me a life.
He looked hurt then, and she regretted the words almost immediately.
That's not what I'm doing.
Then tell me what you are doing.
He took a breath. For a second she thought he would.
Instead, he picked up the envelope.
Trying to make something easier for once.
She let him leave without another argument. She told herself he was an adult. That he had a right to parts of his life that weren't hers. That she could love him without interrogating him.
And all of that was true.
It wasn't the whole truth.
The first job had sounded almost insulting in its simplicity. A man who knew a man asked Cassian to take a sealed parcel across town. Cash on delivery. No questions.
He asked one anyway.
What's inside?
Paperwork.
That's an expensive courier service.
Then enjoy your tip.
He'd needed the money. He'd told himself he would be an idiot to refuse something that ordinary.

The second favor involved waiting in a car while two strangers had an argument inside a building. The third meant driving somebody to a railway station and pretending not to hear the anxious phone call in the back seat. Each job ended with somebody paying him well enough to make the next invitation more difficult to reject.
At first he described them to Ninja as extra shifts. She asked whether the job had dental insurance, and he said it came with a very generous selection of uncomfortable silences.

Months later, in a room above a shuttered shop, a man placed a list of dates in front of him. Cassian recognized every payment. There were signatures and photographs, details he'd never knowingly agreed to leave in anyone's possession.
You've been very reliable.
Cassian looked at the folder.
Is that supposed to be a compliment?
It's an opportunity to continue being reliable.
What if I'm finished?
The man leaned back.
People who are finished don't generally leave so much unfinished business.
Cassian heard the threat in the politeness. He also heard something worse: the suggestion that somebody knew where Ninja lived.
He went home that night and deleted a message he'd started typing to her. It began, *I need to tell you something.* He couldn't find a second sentence that wouldn't put her closer to the danger.
The jobs had begun as favors. The pay was good, and every request came with the promise that it would be the last.
By the time Cassian understood how much other people knew about him, refusing had begun to feel less like a decision and more like a threat.
He didn't tell Ninja.
He couldn't bear to watch the knowledge change the way she looked at him.

There were nights when his phone displayed a number and he stared until it stopped ringing. There were days when he made promises to himself about finishing one final obligation and disappearing from it all.
He told himself that a clean break still existed somewhere.
He only had to reach it.

One afternoon, Cassian sat in his parked car outside a supermarket with the engine off. He had just finished a call with somebody connected to Elias Voss. The caller had agreed, in an almost friendly tone, that of course Cassian could stop working for them.
After one more errand.
Cassian stared at his reflection in the rearview mirror. He looked older than he remembered.
He dialed Ninja's number, waited for her to answer, and listened as she told him—without taking a breath—that her upstairs neighbor had somehow flooded the bathroom by trying to install a shelf.
He laughed. It surprised him.
What's funny?
Nothing. You. The fact that shelving has become a combat sport.
Then she asked if something was wrong.
He gripped the steering wheel.
No. Just wanted to hear your voice.
She went quiet long enough to make him worry he'd frightened her.
Well, you've heard it. It remains incredibly charming.
Debatable.
Come over Sunday. I'll cook.
He wanted to say yes. Instead he promised to try.
When the call ended he sat still for a long time, making a decision he didn't yet know how to carry out: whatever else he had to do, he would find a way to keep those people away from her.
The last time Ninja had dinner with Cassian, he turned up carrying a badly wrapped parcel and an apology.
Before you ask, yes, the wrapping was done by a human being.
A drunk one?
An artist. Unappreciated in his time.

Inside was an old portable music player, the same model she'd once loved and broken years earlier. Cassian had repaired it, or persuaded somebody who actually knew what they were doing to repair it, and loaded it with songs they used to play too loudly in the kitchen.
She stared at it.
Where did you even find this?
I have mysterious talents.
You have mysterious debts, probably.
The joke landed strangely.
Cassian looked down, just for a second. Then he smiled again.
Both can be true.

They ate pasta sitting on the sofa, argued about whether one of the songs was good or simply nostalgic, and laughed until she nearly spilled her drink when he tried to imitate a singer he had absolutely no business imitating.
Later, as he put on his coat, she noticed him checking his phone.
You okay?
Yeah.
That sounded rehearsed.
Everything's all right. Nin.
She moved closer.
For a moment she considered making him stay, demanding an explanation, refusing to let him hide behind his usual jokes.
But he looked so tired.
Call me tomorrow.
He tucked the phone away.
I will.
And don't do anything stupid.
You're taking all my hobbies away.
She hugged him at the door. He held on a fraction longer than usual.
Then he stepped back, touched her cheek lightly, and smiled in the familiar crooked way that had been making terrible things seem manageable since she was a child.
Lock up behind me, menace.
She rolled her eyes.
I always do.
He waited until he heard the lock turn.
It was such a small thing. The two of them had repeated it a hundred times.
She would spend years wishing she'd opened the door again.
Three evenings later, someone knocked.
Ninja was standing at the sink, rinsing a mug. She remembered that detail afterward because it was the sort of useless thing memory kept when the important parts became impossible.
The tap was running.
A small patch of sunlight fell across the counter.
Her phone was on the table, face up.
She turned off the water and went to the door.
Two people stood outside. Dark coats, careful expressions, the uneasy stillness of strangers who had rehearsed what they were about to say.
Are you Cassian's sister?
Everything in her body seemed to recognize the question before her mind did.
Why?
They asked to come inside.
She didn't move.
What happened?
One of them said her name. The other looked toward the stairs.

They said Cassian had been killed. They said there appeared to have been a robbery. They said an investigation was ongoing, though there were indications he had simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.
The words passed through the doorway in neat, impossible pieces.
Killed?
I'm very sorry.
Where?
They told her.
Was he alone?
A pause.
We're still establishing exactly what occurred.
Did he call anyone? Did he say anything?
We don't have that information.
She looked from one face to the other.
They were gentle. They sounded certain about some things and strangely evasive about others.
It made no sense.
Cassian would have called. Cassian would have argued. Cassian would have found a way to say something ridiculous and then come home with a bruise and an apology.
There was no world in which he simply stopped.
When can I see him?
The older one inhaled slowly.
She hated that, too.
The mug remained in the sink. She eventually let them in, answered questions, accepted a number to call.
She didn't cry while they were there.
She wasn't holding herself together. She hadn't yet understood there was something to fall apart.
After they left, she found the phone on the table and called Cassian.
His voicemail answered.
She listened to his voice all the way through.
Then she called again.
And again.
The fourth time, she put the phone down without ending the call and sat on the kitchen floor.
The voicemail continued speaking into an empty room.
You said you'd call tomorrow. You always called. I don't understand how the world can keep moving when you've stopped. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with all the things I haven't told you.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: There was a funeral.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: People brought flowers. Some brought food. Others brought stories she hadn't heard before, most of them kind and almost all of them unbearable.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Someone called Cassian a good man.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Ninja believed that.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Someone else said that at least he hadn't suffered.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: They couldn't possibly know that.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: After the service, a distant acquaintance pressed a folded photograph into her palm. It showed Cassian at a barbecue, grinning with his eyes closed, holding a plate overloaded with food. Ninja had never seen it.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: He's smiling like that because someone dared him to eat everything.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: The woman smiled uncertainly.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: He was always making people laugh.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Ninja looked at the picture again. Cassian's left sleeve was rolled up unevenly. There was a sauce stain on his shirt. It was so completely him that her throat closed.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: He was.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Later, back at home, she set that photograph beside the old music player. She was furious that the world had kept photographs and hadn't kept him. The anger embarrassed her until she stopped caring whether it was reasonable.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She looked down at her hands because she didn't trust what might happen if she answered.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Grief didn't look like the collapse people expected. It looked like reaching for her phone to tell him something funny. Buying too much food. Leaving his messages unread because, for one impossible second, the notification made her believe he might answer.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She slept badly. She became angry at ordinary conversations.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: A friend asked whether she had considered speaking to someone about it.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: About what?

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: About Cassian.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: What would you like me to say?

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: I just thought—

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: I know what you thought.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Her friend went quiet.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Ninja apologized later, but she didn't let the woman back inside the apartment.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: It was easier that way. If nobody came close enough to ask, she didn't have to explain the enormous, shapeless absence in the middle of every day.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: The official account never sat right.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: A robbery. A bad place. Bad timing.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Cassian had sometimes gone out late and come back strange. She remembered the envelope, the unanswered questions, the look on his face when she'd jokingly mentioned debts.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She wondered if there had been something he was afraid to tell her.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Then she hated herself for wondering.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Dead people couldn't defend themselves against suspicion. They couldn't explain. They couldn't say, No, Nin, you've got it wrong.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She asked for information and received little. The questions grew heavier without becoming clearer.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Eventually she stopped asking out loud.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: But she never stopped thinking about them.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Months passed. She saw him everywhere: outside the coffee shop, leaning against familiar railings, reflected in bus windows that belonged to strangers.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: The city was full of places that remembered him.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: And she was exhausted by being expected to remember him in the acceptable ways.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: One afternoon, she tried to make his favorite pasta sauce from memory.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She knew he'd never used a recipe. He'd tasted it, added a little more of something, and announced that the essential ingredient was artistic instinct.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Her attempt was watery and far too salty.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She sat down to eat anyway.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Halfway through the meal, the words slipped out.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Cass, this is disgusting.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: There was no answer.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She pushed the plate away and cried—not because of the sauce, but because she'd expected his reply before she remembered there couldn't be one.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: One evening she opened the old music player.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: The first song started through a pair of headphones.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Cassian had named the playlist FOR THE SMALL MENACE.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: She laughed, one startled, broken sound.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: Then she cried so hard she had to put the player down.

events.section: A House Full of Missing Things
events.text: It was the first time she'd allowed herself to do both in the same moment.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The first time Ninja returned to Cassian's apartment after the funeral, she stood outside the door for eleven minutes.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She knew because she watched the numbers change on her phone. The display was cracked at one corner. Cassian had offered to replace it twice, and twice she'd refused because it worked perfectly well. He would have been insufferably pleased to discover that the screen still worked even when she felt as though nothing else did.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She had his key in her palm.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: For years, the existence of that key had been comforting. It meant there was somewhere she could walk into without knocking, somewhere she'd be welcomed with an insult and a cup of terrible coffee. Now it opened a room that could not answer her.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Eventually she turned the lock.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The apartment smelled faintly of washing powder and the cheap coffee Cassian always bought despite her sustained campaign against it. His jacket hung on the same hook by the door. A half-read paperback lay face down beside the sofa. There was a shopping list on the refrigerator, written in the hurried capitals she remembered from notes he'd left her when they were children.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Bread. Eggs. Batteries. Something green so Ninja stops complaining.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She put her hand over her mouth.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: He had been planning to go shopping.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: It was an absurd thing to find unbearable. A dead man had left a list of things he meant to buy, and suddenly she could see the afternoon he would never have. Cassian standing in a supermarket aisle, looking at two identical cartons and choosing the wrong one. Cassian sending her a photograph of a vegetable and asking whether it counted as something green. Cassian arriving with a bag of food she didn't need, acting as though he'd merely happened to be in the neighborhood.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She sat on the floor and waited for the tightness in her chest to pass.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: It didn't.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: After a while, she began opening cupboards. Not because she was ready to pack anything, but because looking for ordinary objects was easier than standing still.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: He'd kept the cheap ceramic bowl they used to eat cereal from when money was scarce. A chipped corner had been glued back into place years earlier. In a drawer, beneath a tangled collection of phone chargers, she found photographs from a summer they spent trying to pretend a camping holiday hadn't been ruined by rain.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: One showed Cassian sheltering under a ridiculous pink umbrella, grinning as though he had personally invented bad weather.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She remembered that day.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: They'd argued about the directions, eaten sandwiches in the car, and finally given up on the campsite after discovering that their tent leaked from the ceiling. On the drive home, Cassian had made up a deeply unconvincing story about a famous explorer who also gave up on bad weather.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The photo made her smile.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Then she realized that smiling didn't hurt quite as much as the guilt that arrived afterward.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She'd begun to think of grief as a kind of loyalty test. If she enjoyed something, was she leaving him further behind? If she moved his books, was she making the room less his? If she laughed without him, was she becoming somebody he wouldn't recognize?

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She knew how unreasonable those questions sounded.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Knowing didn't make them disappear.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Near the bottom of the desk drawer was a folder of ordinary papers: bills, insurance documents, old warranties. She sorted them into piles because it gave her hands somewhere to be.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: A receipt for a parking garage caught her attention.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She didn't recognize the street. She checked the date. It was from the week before he died.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: There was nothing unusual about a person using a parking garage. Nothing that proved anything. But she remembered the unfamiliar car outside his building and the thick envelope of money he'd insisted was simply from work.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She set the receipt beside the documents the authorities had given her.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: There were so many words in those papers that sounded official and meant almost nothing. An incident at an address. An ongoing investigation. No further details available. A conclusion that seemed to have arrived before any of the questions she wanted answered.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She tried calling the number printed on the letter.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Someone answered with a professional tone and asked for a reference number. Ninja gave it. She explained that she was Cassian's sister. She asked whether there had been witnesses and whether anybody knew why he was in that building.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The person on the telephone was polite. They were also unable to provide more information.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She hung up before she said something she'd regret.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The parking receipt lay between two photographs of her brother. She turned it face down. It was an ordinary bit of paper, and perhaps that was all it would ever be.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: But something about the official explanation had felt wrong from the beginning, and every closed door made that feeling harder to set aside.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: A few days later, one of Cassian's neighbors stopped her in the hallway carrying a basket of laundry.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The woman told Ninja how sorry she was. She said Cassian had sometimes brought her groceries when her knees were bad, and that he had fixed a loose handle on her kitchen cupboard without accepting payment.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Then she asked whether Ninja was moving his things out.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Not yet, Ninja told her.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The woman nodded, but she didn't leave.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: For a moment she looked as though she might say something else. Her eyes moved toward the stairwell, then back to Ninja. Whatever she had been about to mention stayed unsaid.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Instead she squeezed Ninja's hand and went inside.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Ninja stood there with the key still in her fingers.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She wondered how many people carried fragments of Cassian she'd never know. How many knew the gentle version of him, and how many knew the worried man he'd become. How many things he had done out of love, or fear, or a stubborn conviction that he should handle every problem alone.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: The question was almost worse than the silence.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: That evening she made one careful box. She packed the old camping photographs, the cracked cereal bowl, and the shopping list from the refrigerator. She left the rest in place.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: Before closing the door, she looked around at the room and tried to imagine what Cassian would think of her standing there like a stranger.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: He'd probably tell her to stop looking so miserable and come eat something.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: He'd probably say the same ridiculous thing three different ways until she smiled.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: She shut off the light.

events.section: The Apartment That Still Had His Name
events.text: For the first time, she understood that she might need to leave the city—not because it held too little of him, but because it held him everywhere, and none of those places would let her live without having to say goodbye again.
The idea of leaving came quietly, while she scrolled through jobs, rooms, and places she might afford.
A village in the mountains caught her attention.
Bellwether.
A room over a bakery. A street full of shops. Forest trails nearby. Rain, apparently, as a permanent civic policy.
She studied the photographs. She didn't imagine a village could fix anything.

Cassian would still be dead when she woke up there. Whatever had happened to him would still have happened. She would still know what his voice sounded like and hate that she couldn't hear it again without pressing play.
But nobody there would stop speaking when she entered a room.
Nobody would lower their voice and ask how she was coping, as though grief were an illness with a set of expected symptoms.
Nobody would know to call her Cassian's little sister.
For once, being unknown sounded less like loneliness and more like the possibility of rest.
So she packed.
She kept the old player, the photographs, and the chipped blue mug. She took the jacket he'd once lent her and never asked to have back.
She left other things behind because she could not bear the weight of making decisions about them.
On the morning she drove away, she sat with the engine off for several minutes.
Well. Cass.
She tried to think of what he'd say.
Probably something about checking the tires.
Probably a joke about her sense of direction.
Definitely something annoying.
She smiled despite herself.
Then she started the car.
Somewhere nobody knows him. That's all I asked for. One evening where I can just be the woman ordering a drink, instead of the woman with the dead brother.
Back in Bellwether, rain tapped against Ninja's jacket as she walked past shuttered shopfronts.
Through the bakery window, Ada was wiping down a counter. She raised one hand when she saw Ninja pass.
Ninja returned the gesture.
It was a small exchange, not quite a friendship, and she was grateful for how little it asked of her.
At the corner, a warm light fell across the wet pavement.
The Crooked Lantern.
Its door creaked when she pushed it open. The room smelled of wood polish, damp wool, and the comforting suggestion of something cooking behind the bar.
A few people sat at tables. Someone had left a coat over the back of a chair. A low conversation drifted from near the fire. The place seemed to have no interest in impressing anyone.
Perfect.
The bartender looked up.
Evening.
Whiskey, please.
Any preference?
The one that doesn't ask personal questions.
One corner of his mouth lifted.
That narrows it down surprisingly little.
Then your favorite.
He poured a glass and set it in front of her.
She chose a stool with a good view of the door and her shoulder turned slightly away from the room. Old habits. Not fear, exactly. Just the relief of not offering herself to conversation.
For a few minutes, it almost worked.
The glass was cool beneath her fingertips. Rain slipped down the window. Nobody knew her name. Nobody asked about Cassian.
She let the quiet settle.
Then another glass appeared beside the first.
Ninja looked at it.
She hadn't ordered a second.
The bartender tipped his head toward a far corner.
From the man across the room.
Of course.
Her first instinct was irritation, sharp and reassuringly familiar.
She hadn't driven all this way to be approached by a stranger who thought a drink was an invitation to claim part of her evening.
She could send it back.
She almost did.
But the refusal stalled somewhere between thought and speech.
She stared at her whiskey, annoyed by the hesitation. Once, she might have enjoyed the contest of figuring out a stranger before they figured out her.
That person felt far away.
She lifted her gaze anyway.
He sat alone in the corner, dark clothes against the low light, long hair, a beard, and the kind of stillness that made everyone else's movements seem slightly louder.
He was already looking at her.
Not with the easy confidence she'd expected. There was no smug little smile, no exaggerated charm.
For a fraction of a second, he looked almost startled.
As though he'd done something before he had the chance to talk himself out of it.
That caught her attention.
She studied him in return.
He sat where he could see the exits. His control looked practiced, maintained rather than effortless.
There were people like that. People who carried too much while insisting they were perfectly capable of carrying more.
Near the end, Cassian had sometimes sat that way.
The memory stung without warning.
Ninja's fingers tightened around her glass.
Don't start, she told herself.
You came here to be nobody. Not to collect somebody else's problems.
She could leave the second drink untouched, turn away, and make her wishes clear.
She was exceptionally good at that.
But she was curious about his voice. Whether he belonged here, or whether, like her, he needed somewhere nobody would ask questions.
Who are you?
You look like the kind of man who has an answer prepared for everything, and not one of them is the truth.
Don't start. Don't make somebody else's silence into your problem.
So why haven't you looked away?
The thought made her angry at herself.
She didn't know him. She had no reason to care.
Something in his expression suggested he, too, had once believed that moving far enough might finally outrun the past.
She held his gaze.
A second longer than she meant to.
The man in the corner didn't look away.
Neither did she.
